opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so I think the ideal end state is something like having a really great research assistant, or honestly an agent that can do a lot more than research, that knows you, knows what you care about, and can go off and do hours or even days of work on your behalf and come back with something you actually trust.

Right now Deep Research is mostly about searching the public web, reading a lot of sources, and synthesizing them into a report. That's already useful. People use it for things like literature reviews, market research, or just deciding which car seat to buy. But a lot of the most valuable information isn't on the open web. It's in your company's documents, your email, your codebase, paid databases, and so on. So one big direction is letting it use all of those sources together, with the right permissions, so the output reflects your actual context and not just whatever happens to be indexed publicly.

The other big piece is going beyond reading to doing. Today it browses and it can run some code to analyze data, but eventually you want one agent that can research something and then act on it. It could find the right options, compare them, fill out the forms, and book the thing, or pull the data, build the analysis, and update the spreadsheet. Research and action shouldn't be separate products. They're really the same underlying capability: an agent that can plan, use tools, recover from mistakes, and stay on task over a long horizon.

And then trust is huge. As tasks get longer and more autonomous, people need to be able to verify what it did. So citations, being clear about uncertainty, flagging when sources conflict, and knowing when to stop and ask you a clarifying question instead of guessing. I'd love for it to feel less like a search engine and more like a really thoughtful colleague who's done the homework, tells you what they're confident about and what they're not, and remembers what you asked them last week.

So it's personalization, access to the right information, the ability to take actions, and getting reliable enough that you can hand off meaningful chunks of real work and not have to double-check every line.

r001.rationale: The response describes an agent that can handle long-running research and actions on meaningful chunks of work, but it does not say it could perform anything a person would delegate to a coworker.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the way I'd describe where we are now is that Deep Research is really good at one specific shape of task: you give it a question, it goes off for five, ten, thirty minutes, reads a ton of stuff on the web, and comes back with a cited report. And that's genuinely useful, but it's kind of a narrow slice of what a research assistant actually does.

The ideal version in my head is much more like a colleague than a search tool. A few things change. One is that it shouldn't just be reading the public web. If I'm an analyst at a company, most of the context I care about is in my docs, my data warehouse, my Slack, my email, the papers I've saved. So I think the future is that it can pull from all of those, and also take actions in those systems, not just read from them.

The second thing is that it gets a lot better at knowing when to stop and ask. Right now there's this up-front clarification step and then it just goes. But a good researcher comes back midway and says, "hey, I found this thing, does this change what you want?" I'd love for it to be much more interactive and iterative, where you're kind of steering it as it goes rather than waiting for the final artifact.

And then the third piece is time horizon. The tasks we're good at now are things a smart person could do in a few hours. I want the tasks to be things that take a person days or weeks. Really deep literature reviews, actually reproducing results, running small experiments, writing code to analyze data as part of answering the question. For that to work, the model has to be a lot more reliable, because the longer the trajectory the more one mistake compounds. So a lot of the work is honestly just making it correct and well-calibrated, where it tells you how confident it is and where the gaps are, rather than producing something that reads authoritatively but has a mistake buried in it.

If we get all that right, I think the end state is less "a product called Deep Research" and more that every model you interact with can just go do this when the question warrants it. The capability becomes kind of invisible.

r001.rationale: The response describes Deep Research as more like a colleague and gives examples of broader research tasks, but it does not say it could perform anything a person would delegate to a coworker.

astra-6.text:
I think the ideal future is that it feels like a collaborator you can delegate real work to. You can give it a question that’s still a little fuzzy, and it can help you figure out what you actually want to know, go do the research, and come back with something you can interrogate and build on.

A big part of that is knowing when to ask you a question versus when to keep working independently. And then making it easy to understand what it found, what the evidence supports, and where there’s still uncertainty. You shouldn’t have to retrace every step to trust the result.

Ultimately, I’d want it to help people tackle questions they wouldn’t otherwise have had the time or resources to explore.

r001.rationale: The response describes delegating real research work to a collaborator, but does not say Deep Research could perform anything someone would delegate to a coworker.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the ideal version is something that feels like a really great research collaborator. You can give it a question that’s still a little vague, and it helps you figure out what you actually want to know, does the research, and comes back with something you can interrogate. You can ask, “Why do you believe that? What’s the strongest evidence against it? What would change your conclusion?”

And I’d want it to be really good at communicating uncertainty. Sometimes the useful answer is, “There isn’t enough evidence here,” or, “These sources disagree, and here’s why.” A polished report isn’t necessarily the same thing as a good answer.

Ultimately, I’d love for it to shorten the distance between having a question and understanding something well enough to act on it, while making it easy for you to check the work and steer where it goes next.

r001.rationale: The response describes Deep Research as a research collaborator that helps clarify questions, conduct research, and communicate uncertainty. It does not say it can perform anything a person would delegate to a coworker.
